english: Grandmother, I have come to you. -- Grandson, you have grown. Is your mother well? -- She is well and she sent(?) you wool. Sit with me and I will tell you of the cave. -- My grandfather told me of the cave. -- Your grandfather was a big man and he killed a bear with a stone.

The king calls the men of this house to the assembly. -- When do I go? -- Rise at dawn. -- Why does the king call the men? -- Enemies drove away the village's cows. -- I and my brothers will go. -- Drink mead with me and now go. -- I will drink and praise the giver.

Why, mother, do you work in the house? -- Guests are coming to you from grandmother's village. Kindle the fire and ... put the kettle over (the fire). -- How many guests come? -- Three men and four women. -- Shall I carry water from the spring? -- Carry water and milk the cows. -- I run.

english: Come, dawn has shone and we must (go?). -- Guest, you have come to us. Eat with us. -- I am sated. My wife waits for me. -- Now take this garment; snow is on the hills. -- You are dear to me. May you have good things. -- May the village be well, and come back to us.

Brother-in-law, my yoke broke. Give me your yoke; I will plow my field. -- Take it, and in the evening bring it back. Are your oxen young? -- They are young. -- Now yoke them and do not goad them. -- I will give you grain at the harvest(?).
uncertain: wéǵʰontu 3pl imperative 'let them bring' vs addressee

english: Sister, are you at home? -- I am at home and I weave wool. Come in and sit. -- I won't sit. My cows fled from the pen. Have you seen them? -- I saw cows by the river yesterday. Go quickly, and may the Sky help you. -- I go. May your village be well.
